newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin hopes for G8 as he flies to Denver.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin hopes for G8 as he flies to Denver.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday he hoped Russia would become a full-fledged member of the Group of Seven main industrialised nations after their summit in the U.S. city of Denver.
Speaking shortly before his departure for the summit, which begins on Friday, Yeltsin said: "I very much hope that in Denver it will finally be decided to turn the G-7 into the G-8."
"Such a decision would be a historic one for Russia."

Yeltsin, who has attended five previous G7 summits and has taken part in their political discussions, will this year also participate in talks on selected economic issues. He will be excluded only from a one-hour session on financial matters.
But Russia is not a formal member of the G7, which groups the United States, Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan.

Yeltsin, who was speaking to seven reporters from the G7 countries in an interview later carried by Russia's commercial NTV channel, said the Denver summit would have a broad scope including arms control, social problems and regional conflicts.
He expressed concern over the big gulf that has opened up in post-communist Russia between the haves and have-nots and said his government was working hard to tackle poverty.
"Half of our people, if not more, are for the time being living in poverty...Now all our work is aimed at restoring social justice," he said.

But he hailed the State Duma lower house of parliament's tentative approval on Thursday of the government's draft tax code, which he said was essential for reviving Russia's stagnant economy and luring more foreign investment.
"This is a huge victory for us...This is a big move also for foreign businessmen," Yeltsin said.

Yeltsin, who underwent open heart surgery last November and caught pneumonia in January, has resumed firm control of his vast country in recent months, drafting pro-market liberals into his team to help kickstart stalled reforms.
But he denied a suggestion that his latest bold moves were motivated by a desire to secure his place in the history books.
"I am not thinking of history, I am thinking of the matter in hand and of how this will affect poor and middle-class Russians," Yeltsin said.
